{{Short description|Kind of infinitely long sequence of characters}}
[[File:Fibonacci word cutting sequence.png|thumb|upright=1.2|class=skin-invert-image|The [[Fibonacci word]] is an example of a Sturmian word. The start of the [[cutting sequence]] shown here illustrates the start of the word 0100101001.]]
In [[mathematics]], more specifically in [[combinatorics on words]], a '''Sturmian word''' ('''Sturmian sequence''' or '''billiard sequence'''<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Hordijk | first1 = A. | last2 = Laan | first2 = D. A. | chapter = Bounds for Deterministic Periodic Routing sequences | doi = 10.1007/3-540-45535-3_19 | title = Integer Programming and Combinatorial Optimization | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume = 2081 | pages = 236 | year = 2001 | isbn = 978-3-540-42225-9 }}</ref>) is a certain kind of infinitely long [[string (computer science)|sequence of characters]]. The concept is named after [[Jacques Charles François Sturm]].

Such a sequence can be generated by considering a game of [[English billiards]] on a square table. The struck ball will successively hit the vertical and horizontal edges labelled 0 and 1 generating a sequence of letters.<ref>{{cite book|page=117|title=Recent Trends in Combinatorics: The Legacy of Paul Erdős|year=2009|first1=Ervin|last1=Győri|first2=Vera|last2=Sós|author2-link=Vera T. Sós|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-12004-3}}</ref> This sequence is a Sturmian word.

== Definition ==
Sturmian sequences can be defined strictly in terms of their combinatoric properties or geometrically as [[cutting sequence]]s for lines of irrational slope or codings for [[irrational rotation]]s.  They are traditionally taken to be infinite sequences on the alphabet of the two symbols 0 and&nbsp;1.

=== Combinatorial definitions ===

==== Sequences of low complexity ====
For an infinite sequence of symbols ''w'', let ''&sigma;''(''n'') be the [[complexity function]] of ''w''; i.e., ''&sigma;''(''n'') = the number of distinct [[subword | contiguous subwords (factors)]] in ''w'' of length ''n''. Then ''w'' is Sturmian if ''&sigma;''(''n'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 for all&nbsp;''n''.

==== Balanced sequences ====
A set ''X'' of binary strings is called ''balanced'' if the [[Hamming weight]] of elements of ''X'' takes at most two distinct values.  That is, for any <math>s\in X</math> |''s''|<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''k'' or |''s''|<sub>1</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''k''' where |''s''|<sub>1</sub> is the number of 1s in ''s''.

Let ''w'' be an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s and let <math>\mathcal L_n(w)</math> denote the set of all length-''n'' subwords of ''w''.  The sequence ''w'' is Sturmian if <math>\mathcal L_n(w)</math> is balanced for all ''n'' and ''w'' is not eventually periodic.

=== Geometric definitions ===

==== Cutting sequence of irrational ====
Let ''w'' be an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s.  The sequence ''w'' is Sturmian if for some <math>x\in[0,1)</math> and some irrational <math>\theta\in(0,\infty)</math>, ''w'' is realized as the [[cutting sequence]] of the line <math>f(t)=\theta t+x</math>.

==== Difference of Beatty sequences ====
Let ''w''&nbsp;=&nbsp;(''w''<sub>''n''</sub>) be an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s.  The sequence ''w'' is Sturmian if it is the difference of non-homogeneous [[Beatty sequence]]s, that is, for some <math>x\in[0,1)</math> and some irrational <math>\theta\in(0,1)</math>
:<math>w_n = \lfloor n\theta + x\rfloor - \lfloor (n-1)\theta + x \rfloor </math>
for all <math>n</math> or
:<math>w_n = \lceil n\theta + x\rceil - \lceil (n-1)\theta + x \rceil </math>
for all <math>n</math>.

==== Coding of irrational rotation ====
[[File:Sturmian-sequence-from-irrational-rotation.gif|thumb|upright=0.7|class=skin-invert-image|Animation showing the Sturmian sequence generated by an irrational rotation with ''&theta;''&nbsp;&asymp;&nbsp;0.2882 and ''x''&nbsp;&asymp;&nbsp;0.0789]]
For <math>\theta\in [0,1)</math>, define <math>T_\theta:[0,1)\to[0,1)</math> by <math>t\mapsto t+\theta\bmod 1</math>.  For <math>x\in[0,1)</math> define the ''&theta;''-coding of ''x'' to be the sequence (''x''<sub>''n''</sub>) where
:<math>x_n= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } T_\theta^n(x)\in [0,\theta), \\ 0 & \text{else}. \end{cases}</math>

Let ''w'' be an infinite sequence of 0s and 1s.  The sequence ''w'' is Sturmian if for some <math>x\in[0,1)</math> and some irrational <math>\theta\in(0,\infty)</math>, ''w'' is the ''&theta;''-coding of&nbsp;''x''.

== Discussion ==

===Example===
A famous example of a (standard) Sturmian word is the [[Fibonacci word]];<ref name=deluca1995>{{cite journal | journal=Information Processing Letters | year=1995 | pages=307&ndash;312 | doi=10.1016/0020-0190(95)00067-M | title=A division property of the Fibonacci word | first=Aldo | last=de Luca | volume=54 | issue=6 }}</ref> its slope is <math>1/\phi</math>, where <math>\phi</math> is the [[golden ratio]].

===Balanced aperiodic sequences===
A set ''S'' of finite binary words is ''balanced'' if for each ''n'' the subset ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> of words of length ''n'' has the property that the [[Hamming weight]] of the words in ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> takes at most two distinct values.  A '''balanced sequence''' is one for which the set of factors is balanced.  A balanced sequence has at most ''n''+1 distinct factors of length ''n''.<ref name=Loth2002>{{cite book | last = Lothaire | first = M. | author-link = M. Lothaire | title = Algebraic Combinatorics on Words | url = https://archive.org/details/algebraiccombina0000loth | access-date = 2007-02-25 | year = 2002 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | location = Cambridge | isbn = 0-521-81220-8 | chapter = Sturmian Words | zbl = 1001.68093 | chapter-url = http://www-igm.univ-mlv.fr/%7Eberstel/Lothaire/ChapitresACW/C2.ps | url-access = registration }}</ref>{{rp|43}}  An '''aperiodic sequence''' is one which does not consist of a finite sequence followed by a finite cycle.  An aperiodic sequence has at least ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 distinct factors of length ''n''.<ref name=Loth2002/>{{rp|43}}  A sequence is Sturmian if and only if it is balanced and aperiodic.<ref name=Loth2002/>{{rp|43}}

===Slope and intercept===
A [[sequence]] <math>(a_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}</math> over {0,1} is a Sturmian word if and only if there exist two [[real number]]s, the ''slope'' <math>\alpha</math> and the ''intercept'' <math>\rho</math>, with <math>\alpha</math> [[Irrational number|irrational]], such that

:<math>a_n=\lfloor\alpha(n+1)+\rho\rfloor -\lfloor\alpha n+\rho\rfloor-\lfloor\alpha\rfloor</math>

for all <math>n</math>.<ref name=Allo2003>{{cite book | last1 = Allouche | first1 = Jean-Paul | last2 = Shallit | first2 = Jeffrey | author2-link = Jeffrey Shallit | isbn = 978-0-521-82332-6 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | title = Automatic Sequences: Theory, Applications, Generalizations | year = 2003 | zbl=1086.11015 }}</ref>{{rp|284}}<ref name=Fogg2002>{{cite book | last=Pytheas Fogg | first=N. | editor1-first=Valérie | editor1-last = Berthé |editor1-link = Valérie Berthé| editor2-last = Ferenczi | editor2-first= Sébastien | editor3-last= Mauduit | editor3-first= Christian | editor4-last= Siegel | editor4-first= A. | title=Substitutions in dynamics, arithmetics and combinatorics | series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics | volume=1794 | location=Berlin | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | year=2002 | isbn=3-540-44141-7 | zbl=1014.11015 }}</ref>{{rp|152}} Thus a Sturmian word provides a [[discretization]] of the straight line with slope <math>\alpha</math> and intercept&nbsp;''&rho;''.  Without loss of generality, we can always assume <math>0<\alpha<1</math>, because for any integer ''k'' we have

: <math>\lfloor(\alpha + k)(n + 1) + \rho\rfloor - \lfloor(\alpha+k)n + \rho\rfloor - \lfloor\alpha + k\rfloor = a_n.</math>

All the Sturmian words corresponding to the same slope <math>\alpha</math> have the same set of factors; the word <math>c_\alpha</math> corresponding to the intercept <math>\rho=0</math> is the '''standard word''' or '''characteristic word''' of slope <math>\alpha</math>.<ref name=Allo2003/>{{rp|283}} Hence, if <math>0<\alpha<1</math>, the characteristic word <math>c_\alpha</math> is the [[first difference]] of the [[Beatty sequence]] corresponding to the irrational number <math>\alpha</math>.

The standard word <math>c_\alpha</math> is also the limit of a sequence of words <math>(s_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> defined recursively as follows:

Let <math>[0; d_1+1, d_2, \ldots, d_n, \ldots]</math> be the [[continued fraction]] expansion of <math>\alpha</math>, and define
* <math>s_0=1</math>
* <math>s_1=0</math>
* <math>s_{n+1}=s_n^{d_n}s_{n-1}\text{ for }n>0</math>
where the product between words is just their [[concatenation]]. Every word in the sequence <math>(s_n)_{n>0}</math> is a [[Prefix (computer science)|prefix]] of the next ones, so that the sequence itself [[Limit of a sequence|converges]] to an infinite word, which is <math>c_\alpha</math>.

The infinite sequence of words <math>(s_n)_{n \ge 0}</math> defined by the above recursion is called the '''standard sequence''' for the  standard word <math>c_\alpha</math>, and the infinite sequence ''d'' = (''d''<sub>1</sub>, ''d''<sub>2</sub>, ''d''<sub>3</sub>, ...) of nonnegative integers,  with ''d''<sub>1</sub> ≥ 0 and ''d''<sub>''n''</sub> > 0 (''n'' ≥ 2), is called its '''directive sequence'''.

A Sturmian word ''w'' over {0,1} is characteristic if and only if both 0''w'' and 1''w'' are Sturmian.<ref name=BS1994/>

===Frequencies===
If ''s'' is an infinite sequence word and ''w'' is a finite word, let μ<sub>''N''</sub>(''w'') denote the number of occurrences of ''w'' as a factor in the prefix of ''s'' of length ''N''&nbsp;+&nbsp;|''w''|&nbsp;−&nbsp;1.  If ''μ''<sub>''N''</sub>(''w'') has a limit as ''N''→∞, we call this the '''frequency'''  of ''w'', denoted by ''μ''(''w'').<ref name=Loth2002/>{{rp|73}}

For a Sturmian word ''s'', every finite factor has a frequency.  The [[three-gap theorem]] implies that the factors of fixed length ''n'' have at most three distinct frequencies, and if there are three values then one is the sum of the other two.<ref name=Loth2002/>{{rp|73}}

==Non-binary words==
For words over an alphabet of size ''k'' greater than 2, we define a Sturmian word to be one with complexity function ''n''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1.<ref name=Fogg2002/>{{rp|6}}  They can be described in terms of cutting sequences for ''k''-dimensional space.<ref name=Fogg2002/>{{rp|84}}  An alternative definition is as words of minimal complexity subject to not being ultimately periodic.<ref name=Fogg2002/>{{rp|85}}

==Associated real numbers==
A real number for which the digits with respect to some fixed base form a Sturmian word is a [[transcendental number]].<ref name=Fogg2002/>{{rp|64,85}}

==Sturmian endomorphisms==
An endomorphism of the [[free monoid]] ''B''<sup>&lowast;</sup> on a 2-letter alphabet ''B'' is '''Sturmian''' if it maps every Sturmian word to a Sturmian word<ref name=LotII83>{{harvtxt|Lothaire|2011|p=83}}</ref><ref name=PF197>{{harvtxt|Pytheas Fogg|2002|p=197}}</ref> and '''locally Sturmian''' if it maps some Sturmian word to a Sturmian word.<ref name=LotII85>{{harvtxt|Lothaire|2011|p=85}}</ref>  The Sturmian endomorphisms form a submonoid of the monoid of endomorphisms of ''B''<sup>&lowast;</sup>.<ref name=LotII83/>

Define endomorphisms φ and ψ of ''B''<sup>&lowast;</sup>, where ''B'' = {0,1}, by φ(0) = 01, φ(1) = 0 and ψ(0) = 10, ψ(1) = 0.  Then ''I'', φ and ψ are Sturmian,<ref name=LotII84>{{harvtxt|Lothaire|2011|p=84}}</ref> and the Sturmian endomorphisms of ''B''<sup>&lowast;</sup> are precisely those endomorphisms in the submonoid of the endomorphism monoid generated by {''I'',φ,ψ}.<ref name=PF197/><ref name=LotII85/><ref name=BS1994>{{cite journal | last1=Berstel | first1=J. | last2=Séébold | first2=P. | title=A remark on morphic Sturmian words | journal= RAIRO Theoretical Informatics and Applications| volume=8 | number=3–4 | pages=255–263 | year=1994 | issn=0988-3754 | zbl=0883.68104 | doi=10.1051/ita/1994283-402551 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

A morphism is Sturmian if and only if the image of the word 10010010100101 is a [[balanced sequence]]; that is, for each ''n'', the [[Hamming weight]]s of the subwords of length ''n'' take at most two distinct values.<ref name=PF197/><ref name=BS1993>{{citation | chapter=A characterization of Sturmian morphisms | first1=Jean | last1=Berstel | first2=Patrice | last2=Séébold | title=Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science 1993. 18th International Symposium, MFCS'93 Gdańsk, Poland, August 30–September 3, 1993 Proceedings | editor1-first=Andrzej M. | editor1-last=Borzyszkowski | editor2-first=Stefan | editor2-last=Sokołowski | pages=281–290 | year=1993 | doi=10.1007/3-540-57182-5_20 | isbn=978-3-540-57182-7 | series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume=711 | zbl=0925.11026 }}</ref>

== History ==
Although the study of Sturmian words dates back to [[Johann III Bernoulli]] (1772),<ref>[[Johann III Bernoulli|J. Bernoulli III]], Sur une nouvelle espece de calcul, Recueil pour les Astronomes, vol. 1, Berlin, 1772, pp. 255–284</ref><ref name=Allo2003/>{{rp|295}} it was [[Gustav A. Hedlund]] and [[Marston Morse]] in 1940 who coined the term ''Sturmian'' to refer to such sequences,<ref name=Allo2003/>{{rp|295}}<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Morse | first1 = M. | author-link = Marston Morse| last2 = Hedlund | first2 = G. A. | author-link2 = Gustav A. Hedlund| title = Symbolic Dynamics II. Sturmian Trajectories | journal = American Journal of Mathematics | volume = 62 | issue = 1 | pages = 1–42 | doi = 10.2307/2371431 | jstor = 2371431| year = 1940 }}</ref> in honor of the mathematician [[Jacques Charles François Sturm]] due to the relation with the [[Sturm comparison theorem]].<ref name=Fogg2002/>{{rp|114}}
